# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a history of heart valve abnormalities, specifically a concern regarding his heart valve.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experienced difficulty with feeding, requiring short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a history of brain-related issues, specifically a concern regarding his tethered cord.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences blurred vision, which could be attributed to astigmatism.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems, including astigmatism and short- or long-sightedness.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has large front teeth that are sensitive, and proper tooth care is being maintained to prevent further issues.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires additional help in school, particularly in mainstream secondary school, and may need to transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits behavioral differences, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and short fingers with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient needs regular dental check-ups to maintain proper tooth care and prevent further issues.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient should undergo regular hearing reviews to age 5 to monitor potential hearing issues.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient should have regular eye examinations to address vision problems, including astigmatism and short- or long-sightedness.
d) Palate review: The patient should be referred for a palate review if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.
e) Cardiac review: The patient should undergo a cardiac review, including echocardiography and electrocardiogram (ECG), to assess heart conditions.
f) Tethered cord review: The patient should be considered for a tethered cord review if clinical concerns arise, especially if a sacral dimple is present.
g) Growth monitoring: The patient's growth velocity should be monitored, and if height is below the 2nd centile, referral for endocrine investigations should be considered within the context of familial heights.
h) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: The patient may benefit from various therapies, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences difficulty keeping up with peers during physical activities, particularly with simple games like tag, which leaves her feeling exhausted and struggling to maintain energy levels.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has feeding difficulties, refusing certain foods and having trouble swallowing others. Some days are better than others, leading to chronic stress for the parent.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss, making it harder for them to hear and understand spoken language.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits hypotonia, with stiff muscles affecting her movement and preventing her from walking or running like other children her age.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Hypotonia is a common feature in KBG syndrome, characterized by reduced muscle tone and strength, which can impact various aspects of motor function and coordination.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a curvature of the spine (scoliosis) which is mild but requires ongoing monitoring to prevent progression.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 11% of people with KBG syndrome have tethered cord, which can cause pain, weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait. Most children with KBG syndrome do not have these issues.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems, specifically astigmatism and short- or long-sightedness (myopia and hypermetropia), which can worsen speech delay.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss, making it harder for them to hear and understand spoken language.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has weak enamel and needs to be very careful about what she eats and drinks, avoiding sugary snacks and acidic foods.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss, making it harder for them to hear and understand spoken language.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient faces challenges in reading and understanding written materials due to her difficulty seeing distant objects, requiring close-up reading to compensate.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss, making it harder for them to hear and understand spoken language.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient shows behavioral differences, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety, which may require medication.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss, making it harder for them to hear and understand spoken language.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, which can result in an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and short fingers with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: To ensure proper tooth health and prevent cavities.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: To monitor hearing status and address potential issues early.
c) Ophthalmology review: To check for vision problems and ensure timely treatment of refractive errors.
d) Palate review: To assess speech development and feeding issues, especially if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns.
e) Cardiac review: Including echocardiography and electrocardiogram (ECG) to rule out heart conditions and monitor overall cardiovascular health.
f) Skeletal review: X-rays of the wrist, hips, spine, and skull to evaluate bone age and detect any abnormalities.
g) Monitoring growth velocity: If height is below the 2nd centile, refer for endocrine investigations to rule out growth hormone deficiency.
h) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: To address motor function, communication, and emotional needs, respectively.

Some children have undergone surgery, while others have just needed monitoring.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty feeding, requiring short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds. Lack of interest in feeding can be significant and long-lasting.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient's fontanel did not close correctly, and she needs to wait and see if it resolves on its own.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 11% of children with KBG syndrome have tethered cord, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and treatment can include patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery to bring the eyes into line.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

a) How this affects the patient: The patient has cold foods and drinks hurting her teeth, feeling sensitive.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school. b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient faces challenges with chewing tougher foods, adjusting meal times to ensure safe consumption, and potentially experiencing swallowing difficulties.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits a difference in how she walks and runs, stumbling more frequently, and moving a bit differently compared to her peers. Additionally, she finds it challenging to express herself verbally, making communication efforts difficult.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient squints when looking at close-up objects, indicating potential visual strain. This issue persists even in quiet environments and becomes increasingly problematic with background noise.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a higher likelihood of developing vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and treatment involving patches, exercises, glasses, and surgery to align the eyes.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty chewing tough foods, which requires adjustments in meal times to ensure safety. She also experiences swallowing difficulties.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires additional help in school, particularly in mastering developmental milestones such as rolling, sitting, walking, playing with toys, using cutlery, using zips and buttons, and toilet training. Some children may attend special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient shows behavioral differences, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety. Medication may be appropriate in some circumstances.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, leading to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis). Babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle). Some children have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others need monitoring.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Seizures: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which typically respond to standard antiepileptic medications. In some cases, epilepsy may be difficult to treat.
b) Hearing: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss. Children may require multiple airway tubes (grommets) and sometimes hearing aids. Regular hearing checks should be conducted until age 5.
c) Eyesight: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have vision problems such as astigmatism, myopia, hypermetropia, and squint. Treatment includes patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery to correct alignment.
d) Undescended testes: Many boys with KBG syndrome are born with testicles that have not fully descended into the scrotum. In some cases, the testes may descend on their own, but if they don't, they can be surgically brought down and fixed in the scrotum.
e) Skeletal: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have an unusual structure of their spinal bones, leading to scoliosis. Babies may experience a delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle. Some children have short fingers with clinodactyly.
f) Teeth: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have large front teeth and other dental concerns, such as weak enamel and the need for regular dental check-ups.
g) Feeding: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, requiring short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds. Lack of interest in feeding can be significant and long-lasting.
h) Cardiac: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome do not have a very serious heart condition, but a study of 40 European patients showed that 15/40 (38%) had heart conditions. These included changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some required surgery, while others needed monitoring.
i) Tethered cord: One study found that 11% of children with KBG syndrome have tethered cord, which can cause pain, weakness, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait. Most children without these issues do not have them.
j) Palate: While most do not have very significant anomalies of the roof of the mouth, a proportion have subtler anomalies affecting speech development and feeding, suggesting referral for specialist review in some cases.
k) Management Recommendations:
   - Regular dental check-ups
   - Regular hearing reviews to age 5 (even if earlier reviews give a clear response)
   - Ophthalmology review
   - Consider a palate review if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns
   - Referral for a cardiac review following diagnosis, including echocardiography and electrocardiogram (ECG)
   - If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated
   - Consider a skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist, hip, spine, and skull) in children following diagnosis
   - Monitoring growth velocity: if height is below the 2nd centile, consider referral for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights
   - Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy.

Parent: Chewing harder foods has proven challenging for our daughter due to some dental issues we're still trying to fully understand. Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Honestly, I'm getting a bit overwhelmed with all these questions... Okay, focus... Right, her vision. Yes, she struggles to see the board at school, and it's been affecting her learning, I think. She often squints and leans forward to try and get a better look.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Oh dear, I'm so worried about her hearing too... She seems to hear some sounds but not others clearly. It's like she's tuning in and out, you know? And it's hard to know if she's just not listening or if there's really something wrong with her hearing.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Teeth... right... She has trouble chewing harder foods, like apples or carrots. We've had to cut them up into smaller pieces or cook them longer to make them softer. It's been a real challenge at mealtime.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Her heart... yes... There's a structural abnormality, the doctors said. I'm not entirely sure what that means, but they're monitoring it closely. We go back for check-ups regularly.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Epilepsy... that's what they call it. She has seizures sometimes, and we have to be very careful and prepared. It's scary, but we're managing it with medication and lifestyle changes.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Constipation... yes... That's been an issue. She has trouble going to the bathroom regularly, and we've tried different diets and remedies to help her go more smoothly. It's not consistent, but it's definitely a concern.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Developmentally... she seems behind other children her age. The doctors say it's not just one thing, but a combination of factors. We're working with therapists and educators to give her the support she needs.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a structural abnormality in her heart, which requires close monitoring.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences constipation, making it challenging to maintain a regular bowel routine.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome struggle with constipation, requiring dietary adjustments and sometimes additional interventions like medications or supplements.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has epilepsy, which necessitates careful management with medication and lifestyle changes.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which require treatment with antiepileptic drugs.

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits developmental delays and behavioral differences, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome exhibit ASD, ADHD, or anxiety, and around 38% have a structural abnormality in their heart.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient struggles with hearing, particularly distinguishing between different sounds, and may have difficulty focusing on auditory stimuli.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have hearing difficulties, including recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can lead to conductive hearing loss.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems, including astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and possible speech and feeding difficulties.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have vision problems, including astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and possible speech and feeding difficulties.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has trouble chewing harder foods and requires cutting them into smaller pieces or cooking them longer to make them softer.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have difficulty chewing, and around 20-40% struggle with constipation, making it challenging to maintain a regular bowel routine.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient shows developmental delays and behavioral differences, requiring support from therapists and educators to meet her needs.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome show developmental delays and behavioral differences, requiring support from therapists and educators to meet their needs.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome exhibit ASD, ADHD, or anxiety, and around 38% have a structural abnormality in their heart.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, leading to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and short fingers with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have an unusual structure of their spinal bones, leading to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and short fingers with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient should have regular dental check-ups to ensure proper tooth care and prevent cavities.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient should undergo regular hearing reviews to detect potential hearing issues early and address them promptly.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient should have regular ophthalmology reviews to monitor vision problems and provide timely intervention if necessary.
d) Palate review: The patient should be referred for a palate review if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns, as these can impact communication and nutrition.
e) Cardiac review: The patient should undergo a cardiac review, including echocardiography and electrocardiogram (ECG), to monitor the structural abnormalities in her heart.
f) Tethered cord review: If clinical concerns arise regarding the patient's spinal cord, a MRI scan should be considered to assess for tethered cord, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait.
g) Growth monitoring: The patient's growth velocity should be monitored, especially if height is below the 2nd centile, as this may indicate underlying hormonal imbalances or other health issues.
h) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: Given the patient's developmental delays and behavioral differences, comprehensive support through various therapies is recommended to aid in her overall development and quality of life.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a valve abnormality in her heart that the cardiologist is monitoring. This has not caused significant problems so far but regular check-ups are recommended to ensure everything stays under control.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery while some just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty swallowing certain textures and requires work with a specialist to find foods that agree with her.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences seizures, which are not very frequent but can be quite scary. The neurologist is working with the family to manage them better.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient struggles with clarity when trying to talk, sometimes making it hard for others to understand her due to pronunciation issues. Speech therapy is being used to help improve her communication skills.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long-sightedness (myopia and hypermetropia). Squint (strabismus) can also be a feature. Treatment includes patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery to bring the eyes into line.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs to take better care of her teeth by limiting sugary snacks and ensuring regular brushing.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school. The extra demands of mainstream secondary school may prove too challenging, and children may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety. Medication(s) may be appropriate in some circumstances.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones which can give rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis). Babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle). Many people with KBG syndrome have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly). A small number of children have had hip dysplasia, in which the hip joints are easily dislocated.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual anti-epileptic treatments.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient needs to take better care of her teeth by limiting sugary snacks and ensuring regular brushing.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5 (even if earlier reviews give a clear response): The patient has had issues with fluid in her ear, and regular checks are recommended to prevent potential permanent damage.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism and short- or long-sightedness (myopia and hypermetropia), and treatment includes patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery to bring the eyes into line.
d) Check position of testes in boys: The patient's testicles have not completed their journey from the tummy (abdomen) to the sack (scrotum) (cryptorchidism), and they can be brought down and fixed in the scrotum with a simple surgical operation (orchidopexy).
e) Skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist (to determine bone age), hip, spine and skull): Children following diagnosis should undergo this review to assess the patient's skeletal health.
f) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review: The patient's hips may be asymmetrical, and the gait may be painful, prompting medical review.
g) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord (MRI) where clinical concerns arise on an individual basis (especially if sacral dimple is present): The patient may have tethered cord, which can cause pain and weakness in the legs, urinary and bowel issues, sacral dimple, and an unusual gait.
h) Monitor growth velocity: If the patient's height is below the 2nd centile, refer for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights.
i) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: The patient's communication skills may be impacted, and additional therapies may be beneficial.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a congenital heart defect involving the heart valve, requiring regular appointments for monitoring.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences difficulty with bowel movements, leading to challenges in feeding.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has developmental delays and behavioral differences, taking longer than other kids to learn certain skills like walking and sitting.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has recurrent otitis media or glue ear, causing conductive hearing loss, and requires multiple aeration tube insertions and sometimes hearing aids.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and treatment options including patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has weak enamel and needs regular dental check-ups.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and some have short fingers with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Management recommendations: Regular dental check-ups, regular hearing reviews to age 5, eyesight (ophthalmology) review, check position of testes in boys, consideration for a palate review, referral for a cardiac review (including echocardiography and electrocardiogram) following diagnosis, if nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated, consider a skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist, hip, spine, and skull) in children following diagnosis, any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review, consider review and investigation for tethered cord (MRI) where clinical concerns arise on an individual basis (especially if sacral dimple is present), monitor growth velocity: if height is below the 2nd centile consider referral for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights, consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy.
